358.title: Indra returns: the dreamer isn't the self either (8.9–8.10)
358.hook: halfway home, Indra sees the flaw: if the reflection is the self, it goes blind with the body; so he walks back, firewood in hand
358.tomorrow: Indra returns again: not even deep sleep
358.howItsDone: Students in many Hindu traditions return to their teacher with questions again and again; carrying firewood (samit-pani) is the traditional sign of approaching a teacher as a student.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Prajapati, and two students who took a reflection in a pan of water for the self. Your line was the reflection isn't you. Week five of year two begins.
screen: `PRAJAPATI — THE REFLECTION ISN'T YOU.`

segments.voice: A conversation ends, and it went well. Then, about a block later, it hits. Wait. That doesn't make sense. The words replay, the hole gets bigger, and the walking stops. Keep going and let it go, or turn around and admit it didn't land? Indra, king of the gods, has just left his teacher content, and now he's standing on that sidewalk, halfway home.
screen: `FEELING GREAT, THEN A BLOCK LATER.` → `WAIT. THAT DOESN'T MAKE SENSE.` → `KEEP WALKING, OR TURN AROUND?`

segments.voice: On the road, before he reaches the gods, Indra thinks it through. If the self is that reflection, then when the body is well dressed, it's well dressed. When the body is blind, it's blind. When the body is lame, it's lame. When the body dies, it dies. I see nothing good in this. So he turns around and walks back to Prajapati with firewood in his hands, samit-pani, the sign of a student asking to be taught. You left content, Prajapati says. Why are you back? Indra tells him. It is so, Prajapati answers. I'll explain it further. Live here another thirty-two years. The king of the gods signs up for thirty-two more years because one answer didn't hold. Then comes the next teaching: the one who moves about happily in dreams, that is the self. Better, surely. The dreamer isn't blind when the body is blind, isn't lame when the body is lame. Indra leaves, content again. And again, on the road, the doubt comes. In dreams, it's as if someone is killing him, chasing him. It's as if he feels pain. He even weeps, as it were. I see nothing good in this either. So, once more, he turns around. Notice the pattern. Prajapati doesn't give the whole answer at once. He gives an answer good enough to test, and waits for the student to find its edge. The teaching isn't only in the answers. It's in Indra's willingness to walk back.

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice the pictures that start on their own, a memory, a plan, a little scene, like a dream but awake. Don't follow them; notice that a picture is showing and something is aware of it, and when a scene pulls you in, step back to the one aware of the dream.
Indra returns. The king of the gods walks back to his teacher, twice, because the reflection and then the dreamer didn't hold up.

359.title: Indra returns again: not even deep sleep (8.11–8.12)
359.hook: deep, dreamless sleep seems like the answer, until Indra notices that nobody is home there; after a hundred and one years, Prajapati finally says it
359.carry: the one who sees through the eye
359.tomorrow: the horse sacrifice as the cosmos
359.howItsDone: Many Vedanta teachers end their teaching of the Chandogya with Prajapati's instruction to Indra, and the inquiry into the seer behind the senses is central to Hindu contemplative practice, including the modern self-inquiry taught by Ramana Maharshi.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indra walked back to his teacher, because the dreamer, chased and weeping, wasn't the self either. Your line was not the dream.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS — NOT THE DREAM.`

segments.voice: The best sleep of your life. No alarm, no dreams, nothing at all, and you wake up feeling completely new. Ask where you were during those hours, and the answer is: nowhere. I was out. And yet something got you safely from night to morning. Indra has now spent sixty-four years with his teacher. The reflection wasn't the self. The dreamer wasn't the self. So Prajapati tries the deepest rest there is.
screen: `NO ALARM, NO DREAMS.` → `WHERE WERE YOU? NOWHERE.` → `SIXTY-FOUR YEARS SO FAR.`

segments.voice: After another thirty-two years, Prajapati says: when someone is fast asleep, completely at peace, and knows no dream, that is the self. Immortal, fearless. That is Brahman. Indra leaves content, and on the road the doubt comes a third time. In deep sleep, he doesn't know himself as I am this. He doesn't know these beings. It's as if he's been wiped out. I see nothing good in this. Back he goes. This time Prajapati says: live here five more years. Add them up: thirty-two, thirty-two, thirty-two, and five. A hundred and one years. Then, finally, Prajapati speaks plainly. This body is mortal, gripped by death. But it's the dwelling of a self that is deathless and has no body. While you're tied to the body, pleasure and pain hold you. Pleasure and pain don't touch what has no body. Then the line our carry comes from. When the eye looks out into space, the one who is there is the person in the eye. The eye is just for seeing. The one who knows, let me smell this, is the self; the nose is for smelling. Let me speak: speech is for speaking. Let me hear: the ear is for hearing. Let me think: the mind is its divine eye. Look at the journey. Not the reflection, which is seen. Not the dreamer, who suffers. Not deep sleep, where nobody's home. The self is the one who sees through the eye, hears through the ear, thinks through the mind. You never see it, because it's always the one seeing.

segments.voice: Sit with your eyes open, softly, and look at something in front of you: the eye is for seeing, and there's the one who sees. Listen to a sound, then notice a thought, and each time notice the one who hears, the one aware. Don't try to find that one; just rest as it.

360.title: The horse sacrifice as the cosmos (1.1)
360.hook: the Brihadaranyaka, the great forest teaching, opens by turning a king's horse sacrifice into the whole universe: the dawn is its head
360.tomorrow: in the beginning there was nothing
360.howItsDone: The ashvamedha is rarely if ever performed today, but the Brihadaranyaka is studied in Vedic schools of the White Yajur Veda and by Vedanta students, and its opening is often read as a meditation on the world as one sacred body.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, after a hundred and one years, Indra learned the self is the one who sees through the eye. That closed the Chandogya.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS AGAIN — THE ONE WHO SEES THROUGH THE EYE.`

segments.voice: A king's horse, turned loose under guard. That's how tradition describes the start of the ashvamedha, the royal horse sacrifice. The horse wandered, the accounts say, for a year, and the lands it crossed were claimed for the king unless someone fought to stop it. Then came the sacrifice itself. And with this horse, a new Upanishad begins: the Brihadaranyaka. Not with the ritual's rules, though, or its costs. With a vision.
screen: `THE KING'S HORSE, FREE FOR A YEAR.` → `WHEREVER IT WALKS, THE KING CLAIMS.` → `NOT RULES. A VISION.`

segments.voice: Its first words, in Sanskrit, are usha va ashvasya medhyasya shirah. The dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse. Then it keeps going, part by part. The sun is its eye. The wind, its breath. The universal fire, its open mouth. The year is its body. The sky is its back, the air between earth and sky its belly. The stars are its bones, the clouds its flesh, the rivers its entrails, the plants and trees its hair. When it yawns, that's lightning. When it shakes itself, thunder. When it makes water, rain. And its neighing is speech. Read slowly, it's a portrait of the whole world in the shape of one animal. You've seen this move before. The Chandogya took the priest's song and found om inside it. Now the Brihadaranyaka takes a king's great ritual and says: look up. The real horse is already here. Dawn breaks across its head every morning. Its breath is the wind on your face. Some teachers take the passage as a meditation that lets anyone, not only a king, take part in the sacrifice by seeing the world as the horse. Brihadaranyaka means the great forest teaching. It belongs to the White Yajur Veda, and it was taught, tradition says, in the forest, away from the village. In the coming weeks it brings us to Yajnavalkya, and to the philosopher Gargi. But it starts here: at sunrise, with a horse the size of the sky.
screen: `USHA VA ASHVASYA MEDHYASYA SHIRAH.` · `SUN ITS EYE, WIND ITS BREATH.` · `THE REAL HORSE IS ALREADY HERE.` · `THE GREAT FOREST TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE DAWN IS ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Picture the sky at dawn, the first light along the horizon: its head. Feel the air on your skin as its breath, and let the clouds, the rivers you know and the trees outside take their places as its flesh, its entrails, its hair. Breathe slowly, and let the whole world feel like one living body, with you somewhere inside it.
Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice. The Brihadaranyaka opens by seeing the sacrificial horse as the universe: the dawn its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath.

361.title: In the beginning there was nothing; death covered it (1.2)
361.hook: a second creation story, stranger than Uddalaka's: at first there was nothing here at all, covered by death, which is hunger
361.tomorrow: the gods and demons and the breath
361.howItsDone: Hindu scriptures contain many creation accounts, from the Rig Veda's hymns to the Upanishads and Puranas, and teachers generally present them side by side as different windows rather than as a single official version.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashvamedha: the Brihadaranyaka opened by seeing the sacrificial horse as the cosmos. Your line was the dawn is its head.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA — THE DAWN IS ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: In the beginning there was nothing here at all. All this was covered by death. And death, it says, is hunger. That's the first sentence of the Brihadaranyaka's second section. Twenty days ago, Uddalaka told his son a calmer story: in the beginning there was Being alone, and it thought, let me be many. Two great Upanishads, two creation stories. Hindu tradition has kept them both, side by side.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING, NOTHING.` → `TWENTY DAYS AGO: BEING ALONE, CALM.` → `TWO STORIES, KEPT SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit: naiveha kimcanagra asit, mrityunaivedam avritam asit, ashanayaya. Ashanaya hi mrityuh: for hunger is death. Then death does something. It makes a mind, thinking: let me have a self. It moves about, chanting praise, and from its praise water arises. The froth on the water hardens into the earth. Death toils, and from its heat, fire is born. Then it wants a second self, and through the mind it joins with speech. The seed becomes the year; before that, the text says, there was no year. When the year is born, death opens its mouth to swallow it, and the newborn cries out, bhan! That cry becomes speech. Death thinks: if I eat this, I'll have less food. So instead, through speech, it brings forth everything: the verses of the Vedas, the rituals, people, animals. And whatever it brings forth, it begins to eat. Then death longs to offer a greater sacrifice. It toils, its body swells, and the text plays on a word: the swollen one, ashva, the horse. Yesterday's horse, back again. What does it mean that the world comes from hunger? One way to hear it: everything alive wants. Eats, reaches, grows, consumes. The text looks straight at that and says it goes all the way down, to the first stirring of anything at all. In this story, hunger isn't an accident in the world. It's where the world came from.

segments.voice: Notice any wanting in you right now: for food, for your phone, for the sit to end, for something to happen. Don't act on it or push it away; watch it the way you'd watch weather, rising, leaning forward, sometimes fading on its own. Breathe with it.

362.title: The gods and demons and the breath (1.3)
362.hook: the gods audition every sense to sing their victory chant, and only the plain breath can't be corrupted
362.tomorrow: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring
362.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant asato ma sad gamaya at the start of study, worship or a gathering, and teachers often explain its three lines as the movement from death to the deathless.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashanaya: at first there was nothing, covered by death, which is hunger. Your line was from hunger, the world.
screen: `FROM HUNGER, THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Lead me from the unreal to the real. From darkness to light. From death to the deathless. It's chanted in Sanskrit before classes, pujas, yoga sessions, school assemblies. And it comes from today's chapter of the Brihadaranyaka, at the end of a strange little war story. The gods and the demons, both children of the creator Prajapati, are fighting over the worlds. The gods' plan: win with a chant. All they need is a singer the demons can't corrupt. So they start auditioning the parts of the body.
screen: `LEAD ME FROM THE UNREAL TO THE REAL.` → `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?` → `THE GODS NEED A SINGER.`

segments.voice: First they ask speech. Speech sings for them, but keeps the best part for itself: the pleasure of speaking well. The demons rush at it and pierce it with evil. That, says the text, is why we say things we shouldn't. Then smell. Then the eye. Then the ear. Then the mind. Each one sings, keeps something back, and gets pierced. That's why we see, hear and think things we wish we hadn't. Last, the gods turn to the breath in the mouth, the plain breath that keeps you alive. Breath sings. The demons rush at it too, and they shatter, the text says, like a clod of earth thrown against a stone. Why breath? One common reading: it took nothing for itself. It sang for everyone. A few weeks ago, the Chandogya told this same battle in a few lines, and its longer story had breath win by threatening to leave. Here the battle is told in full, and on this reading breath wins because it's the one faculty that doesn't grab. Then breath carries each of the others past death. Speech becomes fire. The eye becomes the sun. The ear becomes the directions. The mind becomes the moon. And the chapter ends with the chant: asato ma sad gamaya, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, mrityor ma amritam gamaya. The text explains its own words. The unreal is death; the real is the deathless. Darkness is death; light is the deathless. In its home, this chant is a prayer to be carried the way breath carries the senses.
screen: `SPEECH SINGS, AND KEEPS SOME FOR ITSELF.` · `EYE, EAR, MIND: EACH ONE PIERCED.` · `THE DEMONS SHATTER ON THE BREATH.` · `ASATO MA SAD GAMAYA.` · then, large: `BREATH IS UNTOUCHED BY EVIL.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move without steering it, and notice how it takes nothing for itself: it comes in, feeds every part of you, and goes. When a thought, a sound or a worry grabs you, let it be, and come back to the breath under it. If you pray, you can say the old chant silently on the out-breath: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless.
Prana, breath, the life-force. In this story prana is the one faculty the demons couldn't pierce, because it sang for everyone and kept nothing back.

segments.voice: Your line: breath is untouched by evil. Tomorrow, the first words ever spoken. Until then.

363.title: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring (1.4)
363.hook: before anything else exists, the self says its first words, then feels its first fear, then its first loneliness
363.tomorrow: the self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world
363.howItsDone: Students of the Upanishads read this passage as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account; in Vedanta teaching it is often paired with aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from the same chapter (1.4.10), one of the great sayings.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gods auditioned every sense, and only prana, the plain breath, couldn't be pierced. Your line was breath is untouched by evil.
screen: `BREATH IS UNTOUCHED BY EVIL.`

segments.voice: A knock on a door. Someone inside calls: who is it? And the answer often comes before any name: it's me. A small habit, easy to miss. The Brihadaranyaka stops to explain it, in the middle of telling how the world began. That habit, it says, goes all the way back to the first moment there was anyone at all: the first words ever spoken, and the two feelings that came right after them.
screen: `WHO IS IT?` → `IT'S ME.` → `THE FIRST WORDS EVER SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: In the beginning, the text says, there was only the self, in the shape of a person. It looked around and saw nothing but itself. And the first thing it said was aham asmi. I am. So it came to be called I. That's why, the text adds, when anyone is called even now, they first say it's me, and then whatever other name they have. Then the self was afraid. That's why, the text says, a person alone is afraid. Then it thought: there's nothing here but me. What am I afraid of? And the fear left. Because, the text says, fear only comes from a second. Then the self had no joy. That's why a person alone has no joy. And it wanted a second. Three moods in a few lines: I am, then fear, then longing. Notice which one thinking can cure. Fear goes the moment the self sees there's nothing else to fear. Loneliness doesn't go that way. It turns into wanting, and the wanting, tomorrow, becomes a whole world. Later Hindu philosophy uses this little word, aham, in two very different ways. Ahamkara, the I-maker, is the ego that says me, mine, my name. And in Advaita Vedanta, the phrase aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from a few lines later in this same chapter, points at an I with no name tacked on after it. The first words in this story come before either reading: just I am, before any other name arrives.
screen: `AHAM ASMI: I AM.` · `FEAR COMES FROM A SECOND.` · `ALONE, IT HAD NO JOY.` · `TWO KINDS OF I.` · then, large: `I AM, BEFORE ANY NAME.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, and notice the plain sense that you're here: not your name, not your job, not whose child or parent you are. Just: I am. If a worry comes, ask it gently, as the self did in the story, what in this room, right now, there is to be afraid of, and then come back to I am.
Aham asmi. I am. In the Brihadaranyaka, the first words the self ever spoke, before there was anything else to speak to.

segments.voice: Your line: aham asmi. Tomorrow, the lonely self finds a way to have a second. Day three hundred sixty-three, done.

364.title: The self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world (1.4)
364.hook: the lonely self makes itself fall in two, and the two halves chase each other through every kind of creature
364.tomorrow: the self is dearer than a son
364.howItsDone: Students read this as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account in chapter one; in many Hindu weddings the couple is spoken of as two halves of one, and the wife is called ardhangini, the half of the body.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, aham asmi: the self alone said I am, then felt fear, then loneliness, and wanted a second.
screen: `AHAM ASMI.`

segments.voice: People still say it at weddings: my other half. It sounds like a greeting card. In the Brihadaranyaka, one of the oldest Upanishads, it isn't a greeting card at all. It's a creation story. The self was alone, and lonely. It wanted a second, and there was no second anywhere. So it did the only thing it could. It used itself.
screen: `MY OTHER HALF.` → `ALONE, AND NOTHING ELSE ANYWHERE.` → `IT USED ITSELF.`

segments.voice: The self, the text says, was as big as a man and a woman holding each other. It made itself fall in two, and from that came husband and wife. The Sanskrit plays on its own words here: the verb for fall is pat, and husband and wife are pati and patni. Then the text quotes the sage Yajnavalkya, whom we'll meet properly in two days: each of us, he used to say, is like half of something split. Translators argue over the exact object, half a shell or half a split pea, but the picture is the same. You are the half, and the empty space beside you is the shape of the other. The two halves joined, and humans were born. Then the story turns strange and wide. She thinks: he made me from himself; how can he join with me? I'll hide. She becomes a cow; he becomes a bull. She becomes a mare; he, a stallion. A she-goat, a goat. A ewe, a ram. And on and on, the text says, down to the ants. Every pair of creatures in the world comes out of that chase. At the end the self knows: I am this whole creation, because I poured it out of myself. So the story is about a marriage, and about much more than a marriage. Everything that comes in twos, wanting and wanted, is the one self looking for itself. Look back at this week: the dreamer, then deep sleep. The horse as the cosmos. Death's hunger making a world. Breath staying clean. I am. And today, the half.
screen: `IT MADE ITSELF FALL IN TWO.` · `PAT, PATI, PATNI.` · `SHE HIDES; HE FOLLOWS, DOWN TO THE ANTS.` · `I AM THIS WHOLE CREATION.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THE HALF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who completes something in you: a partner, a friend, a sibling, a child, someone gone. Notice the space beside you that only they fill, and don't fix or say anything; just let the space be there, and let it be full. If no one comes to mind, rest in the line itself, and notice how much of the world comes in pairs.
Ardha, half. In the Brihadaranyaka, the one self falls into two, and every pair of creatures comes from that split; each of us, Yajnavalkya says, is ardha, half of something split.
